question: You print your desk arm's Jacobian and look at column j. What does it mean?
options: The torque joint j needs to hold the tip still
The tip position when only joint j is bent
The tip velocity per unit speed of joint j
explanation: Column j shows how the tip moves when only joint j turns at unit speed, so it is a tip velocity, not a position or a torque.

question: Your arm holds still while a person pushes its tip. Which relation maps that tip force to joint torques?
explanation: The tip's power F . (J q-dot) must equal the joints' power tau . q-dot, which only works for tau = J^T F. So the tip force reaches the joints through the transpose of J.

question: On your desk arm the analytic and finite-difference Jacobians disagree by 0.3 at a random pose. Most likely cause?
options: Rounding noise from the finite-difference step
The arm is close to a singularity at that pose
A real bug in one of the two Jacobian programs
explanation: Finite-difference rounding noise is only about 1e-10 here, so a gap of 0.3 is far too big for noise and means one of the two programs has a real bug.

question: You check a Jacobian with a central-difference step of 1e-12 rad. What happens?
options: The error now comes mostly from rounding
The curvature error grows and spoils the check
The slope gets better as the step shrinks
explanation: A step of 1e-12 rad changes the tip position so little that the rounding error in that tiny difference outweighs the curvature error, so a smaller step no longer helps.

question: A 2 kg mass hangs from your arm's tip. How do you get the joint torques that hold it?
options: Split the weight force equally across the joints
J^T times the weight force acting at the tip
J times the weight force acting at the tip
explanation: The weight pulls down on the tip as a force, and a tip force reaches the joints through J transposed, so you multiply the weight force by J^T.

question: Your Jacobian test passes at the one pose you tried. Why is that not enough?
options: Jacobians change with time even when the arm holds still
A wrong sign or link order can pass at a symmetric pose
The finite-difference check cannot run at only one pose
explanation: A wrong sign or link order can still give the right answer at a symmetric pose, so one pose proves little. Check many random poses, as with the DH table in lesson 02/01.
